conventions.convention: English diagrams have rows numbered downward and columns rightward. A hook includes its anchor once; h(i,j)=λ_i−j+λ′_j−i+1. The empty hook product is 1.

For distinct real alphabets, standard means an injective filling with strictly increasing rows and columns, identified with the published standard alphabet by increasing rank relabelling. Row insertion bumps the leftmost entry strictly greater than the carried letter.
Reverse deletion starts at a removable box and proceeds upward, replacing the rightmost entry strictly smaller than the carried value; its output includes the expelled letter.

Two-line arrays have positive-integer entries and lexicographically nondecreasing columns; equal top entries require nondecreasing bottom entries. Repeated-letter insertion still bumps strictly greater entries. Reverse recording deletion chooses the rightmost maximum.
Peter–Weyl uses compact Hausdorff groups, normalized Haar probability and AC. Matrix coefficients are ⟨π(k)v,w⟩, linear in v and conjugate-linear in w.

The unitary dual consists of unitary-equivalence classes of nonzero irreducible strongly continuous unitary representations. No topology or countability is asserted; choosing representatives and bases uses AC.
Normalized coefficients are u^π_ij(k)=√d_π⟨π(k)e_i,e_j⟩. The first index specifies the input vector. Schur orthogonality has constant 1/d_π before normalization.

Arbitrary-index square sums are suprema of finite subsums; vector sums converge as finite-subset nets. Strong continuity is tested by neighbourhoods, without countability assumptions on the group or index set.
For c^π_v,w, right translation acts on v by π and left translation acts on w by π, giving right block type π and left block type conjugate π.

The Fourier operator in the Parseval corollary is π(f)=∫f(k)π(k)⁻¹dμ(k), unlike the earlier integrated action ∫f(k)π(k)dμ(k). Inversion is asserted in L², and pointwise exactness only for finite coefficient expansions.
Node content is column minus row; c_T(1)=0 and content vectors list labels 1 through n.
The symmetric-group chain uses labels 1,…,n, with S_m fixing later labels. X₁=0 and X_k=Σ_{j<k}(j k), integrally over every commutative ring.
Seminormal vectors are v_T=P_Tσ_Tv₀, with σ_T carrying the row-filled tableau to T. For r=c_T(i+1)−c_T(i), the coefficient of v_{s_iT} is 1 when s_iT is longer and 1−r⁻² when it is shorter.
Orthogonal normalization divides seminormal vectors by their positive norms; the off-diagonal entry is the positive square root √(1−r⁻²).

load_bearing.statement: For n≥1, X_kv_T=c_T(k)v_T in the Young basis, with one-dimensional joint eigenspaces indexed by standard tableaux. An integer vector (a₁,…,a_n) occurs exactly when a₁=0; for every q>1 at least one of a_q−1,a_q+1 occurs earlier; and whenever a_p=a_q with p<q, both neighbours occur strictly between p and q. Tableau content vectors give a bijection onto this set.

Assume AC. For a compact Hausdorff group K with normalized Haar probability, the normalized irreducible matrix coefficient family is an orthonormal basis of L²(K), and Σ_{π,i,j}|⟨f,u^π_ij⟩|²=‖f‖²₂ for every f∈L²(K).

For n≥0, iterated row insertion with chronological recording is a bijection from permutations of {1,…,n} in one-line form to pairs of standard tableaux of a common shape λ⊢n. Its inverse repeatedly reverse-deletes the box carrying the largest remaining recording label.

Products P_T of the chain's central idempotents along Young paths are nonzero rank-one idempotents, pairwise orthogonal and summing to 1. GZ(n)=⊕_T CP_T is the Young-basis diagonal algebra; the X_k act diagonally, and GZ(n) is maximal commutative in C[S_n].
Assume AC. For every compact Hausdorff group K, every f∈C(K,C) and every ε>0, there is h∈R(K) with sup_{k∈K}|f(k)−h(k)|<ε.

Lexicographically ordered positive-integer two-line arrays correspond bijectively to same-shape semistandard pairs, with bottom and top multisets as their respective contents. The inverse uses rightmost-maximum recording deletion and reverse insertion deletion. Sorting the coordinate-swapped array exchanges P and Q. Top line u_k=k specializes to word insertion with standard Q.

For m≥0 and ν⊢m, the transposition sum T_m is central and acts on the complex Specht module by z_ν=Σ_i binom(ν_i,2)−Σ_j binom(ν′_j,2)=Σ_{(r,c)∈[ν]}(c−r)=n(ν′)−n(ν). For m≥2, χ^ν((1 2))=dim(S^ν)z_ν/binom(m,2); for m=0,1 the scalar and sum are zero.

Starting with P_[1]=1, for n≥2 and predecessor shape μ, P_T=P_prefix ∏_{c∈A(μ),c≠c_T(n)}(X_n−c)/(c_T(n)−c). Denominators are nonzero; these are the rational-polynomial rank-one Young projectors, pairwise orthogonal and summing to 1.

For n≥1 and λ⊢n, choose nonzero v₀ on the row-filled Young line and set v_T=P_Tσ_Tv₀. These form a basis. Same-row and same-column adjacent labels give signs +1 and −1. Otherwise T′=s_iT is standard and |r|>1; when T′ is longer, s_iv_T=v_T′+r⁻¹v_T and s_iv_T′=(1−r⁻²)v_T−r⁻¹v_T′, with the equivalent reversed formulas when T′ is shorter.
For every n≥0 and λ⊢n, f^λ=n!/∏_{x∈[λ]}h(x), with empty product 1. This also equals dim_C S^λ; the empty Specht module has dimension 1, and one-row and one-column tableau numbers are 1.
For λ⊢n, summing the corner-removal hook-product ratios P(λ)/P(λ−x) over removable nodes gives n; the empty partition contributes the empty sum 0.
For a standard tableau T with distinct real entries and distinct real x,y absent from T, (x→T)←y=x→(T←y), as tableaux.
Assume AC. Every strongly continuous unitary representation of a compact Hausdorff group on a nonzero complex Hilbert space contains a nonzero finite-dimensional closed invariant subspace.

concerns.concern: Statement (1) allows arbitrary positive-integer arrays and calls its outputs 'semistandard tableaux' citing def-semistandard-tableau-and-kostka-number. That Definition begins 'Let λ⊢n and μ⊢n be partitions' and requires label i to occur μ_i times. The allowed singleton array ((2);(2)) produces P=Q=[2], whose content counts (0,1) are not a partition. Under the literal supplied definition, the stated output class is therefore unsupported. The proof handles unrestricted weak-row/strict-column fillings, but an explicit unrestricted-content definition or convention is needed. This concerns the library definition domain, not the classical RSK theorem.

Verification 2.1 says 'point separation uses only the finitely many coordinates in which two points differ'. Two points of an arbitrary product may differ in infinitely many coordinates, for example the all-identity and all-nonidentity points of a countable product of groups of order two. Fact F6 already gives the correct argument: one differing coordinate suffices. The density conclusion and its actual separation argument remain valid.

seams_checked.note: Read both page texts and the three actual item suppliers consumed by the circle companion example: the circle/R-Z isomorphism, the character-group definition, and clause (1) compact abelian ⇒ discrete Pontryagin dual. The example's Facts F5/F7 and Verification 2.1 preserve these domains and the one-way implication. Integer-character completeness is supplied separately by the published trigonometric basis theorem. No converse, general LCA separation or biduality is imported. The A page lists the prerequisite but makes no stronger item-level claim from it; the supplier page has no reciprocal Peter–Weyl citation.
